title: Secrets mapping and threat hypotheses — security sync (Oct 18 2026)
content:
Attendees: Aisha P., Samir R., Leah K., Jon P., and guests from infra (Marta B.)

Purpose: quick working session to (1) sanity-check the secrets inventory export from vault, (2) map high-risk secrets to recent deployment topologies, and (3) run a short threat-hypothesis exercise to surface overlooked exposure paths. Not a formal review — notes + action items for follow-up.

Background/context:
- Last secrets sweep (Q2 2026) flagged ~18 stale service tokens; cleanup largely done but we still see noisy secrets attached to older staging clusters.
- New dedicated/private rollout expanded customer-side KMS integrations (ticket JIRA-OPS-302). With more KMS endpoints, the attack surface changes (key metadata endpoints, rotation webhooks).
- Recent internal postmortem (INC-2026-09-14) suggested improving mapping between secret owners and runtime topology to speed triage.

Agenda (30m):
1) Review vault export columns + confidence levels (Aisha)
2) Walk a small set of secret artifacts against deployment maps (Samir + Marta)
3) Threat hypotheses: 4 quick failure modes and likely mitigations (group exercise)
4) Agree next steps and owners

Notes + outcomes:
- Vault export quality: metadata fields missing for ~12% of secrets (no owner label, no service tag). Root cause: older CI jobs wrote secrets without the new label template. See sample rows attached below. (Action: create small script to synth-owner-labels from git history)
- Mapping friction: team discovered that "staging-east-legacy" cluster uses a mix of machine-identity tokens and user-scoped API keys for the same service (model ingestion). This complicates rotation since keys have different lifetimes and ownership. (Decision: treat machine tokens as infra-owned; user API keys as app-owned and plan separate rotation cadence)
- High-risk findings:
  - A set of long-lived mobile SDK API keys (labelled mobile-sdk-prod) used in analytics pipeline. Keys are client-embedded and not rotated. If leaked, they allow ingestion-level access to user-provided prompts (privacy risk). (Mitigation recommended: move ingestion endpoints behind signer service + short-lived tokens)
  - KMS webhook endpoint secrets (used for automated rotation callbacks) were present in vault but lacked IP allowlist metadata. If a webhook secret is leaked and the endpoint is internet-facing, rotation workflows could be abused. (Mitigation: rotate webhooks, require mTLS for callbacks, add service-level allowlist)
  - A developer SSH key found in a legacy shared account (legacy-ops) with sudo access on a small set of build hosts. It is flagged as "critical" until key replaced and session history reviewed. (Action: emergency rotation + session audit, Leah)

Threat hypotheses (fast exercise):
We enumerated 4 plausible exposure paths and rated likelihood/impact (low/med/high):
1) CI artifact leak -> secrets in build logs: likelihood MED, impact MED-HIGH. Notes: build logs sometimes contain templated vars; need to add scrubbers + S3 retention policy. (Owner: Samir, ticket JIRA-SEC-902)
2) Compromised third-party analytics SDK -> exfiltrate ingestion key: likelihood LOW-MED, impact HIGH (PII). Recommendation: disambiguate ingestion vs. control plane keys; reduce permissions. (Owner: Product security, Leah)
3) Misconfigured KMS policy on customer-dedicated clusters -> cross-tenant access: likelihood LOW, impact CRITICAL. Put higher-priority guardrails: automated policy linting on deploy + preflight checks. (Owner: infra-policy, Marta)
4) Developer workstation compromise -> reuse of long-lived tokens: likelihood MED, impact MED. Short-term: enforce ephemeral tokens for non-infra workflows; long-term: move secrets to hardware-backed signing. (Owner: eng-sre)

Decisions made in-session:
- Prioritize rotation of: legacy-ops SSH key, mobile-sdk-prod keys, and KMS webhook secrets.
- Start labeling migration job: create a small service to backfill missing owner/service tags using git history + deployment manifests. Target: Backfill 80% by EOW Oct 25. (Owner: Samir)
- Create a protective preflight check for terraform modules that manipulate KMS policies. Block merges that fail a policy-lint step. (Owner: Marta, ticket JIRA-OPS-310)

Action items (owner, ETA, ticket):
- Emergency rotate legacy-ops SSH key; run session history audit (Leah, 2026-10-19, JIRA-SEC-909)
- Implement build-log scrubber for templated vars; add retention rule (Samir, 2026-11-01, JIRA-SEC-902)
- Backfill secret owner labels script + run on vault export (Samir, 2026-10-25, GH-#128)
- Rotate mobile-sdk-prod keys and replace client flow with signer service blueprint (Product Security + Mobile eng, 2026-11-08, JIRA-PRD-441)
- Add mTLS + IP allowlist for KMS webhook callbacks; add integration tests (Marta, 2026-11-15, JIRA-OPS-312)
- Draft a short-runbook for triage steps when a secret is leaked (include who to page, who can rotate, and communication templates). (Leah, 2026-10-27, CONFLUENCE-SEC-1207)

Open questions / unresolved:
- Scope of the backfill: should we mutate existing secret metadata in-place or create a shadow index (read-only) first? Concerns: audit trail and potential misattribution if backfill guesses wrong. We decided to start with a shadow index and add confirmed labels later.
- Customer-facing KMS integrations: do we require customers to opt-in to webhook callbacks? Product needs to weigh UX vs. risk. (Leah to convene product + compliance)

Follow-ups planned:
- Mini dry-run next week (Oct 25): Samir will run backfill on a small subset and we will validate 10 sample mappings during the sync.
- Full playbook review on Nov 2: incorporate lessons from emergency rotations and test scrubber integration.

Appendix: quick samples from vault export (redacted):
- secret_id: s_92837, name: "analytics/mobile-sdk-prod", created_by: ci-pipeline-legacy, owner: null, tags: ["analytics"], last_access: 2026-08-01
- secret_id: s_77211, name: "kms/webhook/rot-a", created_by: rotation-runner, owner: infra-rotation, tags: ["kms","webhook"], last_access: 2026-10-10

Notes to self: capture a list of pattern rules for the backfill heuristics (git commit history, terraform resource owners, deploy annotations). Avoid aggressive overwrite of any owner labels without cross-check.

If you weren't at the session and want context: skim the tickets JIRA-SEC-902 (logs), JIRA-OPS-310 (policy lint), and CONFLUENCE-SEC-1207 (draft runbook).
